key_cases.holding: As a matter of first impression the division held that the Americans with Disabilities Act does not pre-empt section 19-3-604(1)(b)(I), because the question whether reasonable accommodations could address a parent's mental impairment is subsumed within the statutory question whether an appropriate treatment plan can be devised.
key_cases.relevance: This is the leading Colorado decision on disability discrimination claims in child-welfare proceedings, and it encourages trial courts to make express accommodation findings.
key_cases.quote: we conclude that it does not conflict with the ADA's requirement that a public entity make reasonable accommodations for qualified individuals with disabilities.

key_cases.holding: The division held that a juvenile court must consider reasonable accommodations for a parent's disability in deciding whether the treatment plan was appropriate and whether the department made reasonable efforts to rehabilitate the parent, and affirmed because the court had done so.
key_cases.relevance: This decision supplies the operative Colorado test for disability-based discrimination claims against a county department in a dependency case.
key_cases.quote: a juvenile court must consider reasonable accommodations in deciding whether such a parent's treatment plan was appropriate and whether reasonable efforts were made to rehabilitate the parent.

key_cases.case_name: Malik v. Arapahoe County Department of Social Services
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Tenth Circuit affirmed the denial of qualified immunity, holding that procuring an ex parte child custody order through distortion, misrepresentation and omission, and in retaliation for a parent's retaining counsel, violated clearly established Fourth, First and Fourteenth Amendment rights.
key_cases.relevance: Retaliation against a parent for exercising the right to counsel is actionable under section 1983 as a First Amendment violation.
key_cases.quote: it was clearly established law that, except in extraordinary circumstances, a parent has a liberty interest in familial association and privacy that cannot be violated without adequate pre-deprivation procedures.
